questions.stem: Which name is given to a gas turning into a liquid?

options.text: condensation
options.explanation: Condensation is the gas-to-liquid transition.

options.text: freezing
options.explanation: Freezing is the liquid-to-solid transition.

options.text: evaporation
options.explanation: Evaporation runs the other way, liquid to gas.

options.text: sublimation
options.explanation: Sublimation jumps solid straight to gas.

options.text: freezing and evaporation
options.explanation: Freezing releases energy while evaporation absorbs it.

options.text: melting and boiling
options.explanation: Both loosen particle arrangements and so absorb energy.

options.text: freezing and condensation
options.explanation: Both tighten arrangements and so release energy.

options.text: condensation and melting
options.explanation: Condensation releases energy while melting absorbs it.

questions.stem: Why does the evaporation of sweat cool the skin?

options.text: the water condenses on the skin and cools it
options.explanation: Sweat evaporates rather than condensing; condensation would warm the surface.

options.text: water conducts heat better than skin
options.explanation: The cooling comes from the state change, not from conduction.

options.text: evaporating water absorbs energy from the skin
options.explanation: The most energetic surface molecules leave, taking energy away with them.

options.text: evaporating water releases energy into the skin
options.explanation: Evaporation is endothermic — it takes energy in, it does not give it out.

questions.stem: How does boiling differ from evaporation?

options.text: boiling happens only at the surface at any temperature
options.explanation: That describes evaporation, not boiling.

options.text: boiling absorbs no energy because the temperature is constant
options.explanation: Energy is still absorbed during boiling — it loosens the bonds instead of raising temperature.

options.text: boiling turns a solid directly into a gas
options.explanation: Solid-to-gas is sublimation.

options.text: boiling occurs throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature
options.explanation: Bubbles form everywhere once the boiling point is reached.

questions.stem: A beaker of stearic acid cools from 80 °C to room temperature and solidifies. What happens to the energy stored in the acid during solidification?

options.text: it decreases as energy is released to the surroundings
options.explanation: Freezing is exothermic: forming the lattice exports energy.

options.text: it increases because particles move faster
options.explanation: Cooling slows the particles; the store empties rather than fills.

options.text: it stays constant because temperature is constant during freezing
options.explanation: A constant temperature during freezing does not mean constant energy — latent energy leaves the system.

options.text: it becomes zero when the acid is fully solid
options.explanation: Solid particles still vibrate, so the energy store never empties completely.

questions.stem: State the name of the transition in which a solid changes directly into a gas.
questions.modelAnswer: Sublimation is the direct change from solid to gas without any liquid stage in between.

questions.stem: State whether energy is absorbed or released during freezing, and name the particles' role in that release.
questions.modelAnswer: Energy is released during freezing as the particles settle into fixed positions and new attractions form in the solid lattice.

questions.stem: Explain why heating a sealed flask of liquid may raise its temperature at first but hold it constant once boiling begins.
questions.modelAnswer: Before boiling, the supplied energy goes into the internal store and shows up as faster particles and a higher temperature. Once boiling starts, every further joule is spent pulling particles apart against their attractions — the work of vaporisation — so the internal energy still rises but the temperature stays pinned at the boiling point until the liquid has gone.

questions.stem: A pan of water boils dry on a hot plate. Describe what happens to the temperature of the water during the boiling and state where the heater's energy goes once 100 °C is reached.
questions.modelAnswer: The temperature rises to 100 °C and then stays constant throughout the boiling. Once at 100 °C, the heater's energy no longer raises the temperature — it is absorbed as the energy needed to turn liquid water into steam, loosening the particle arrangement until the last of the water has vaporised.

questions.stem: What is meant by heat as an energy transfer between objects at different temperatures?

options.text: the total mass of the hot object
options.explanation: Mass is irrelevant to the definition of heat.

options.text: energy transferred because of a temperature difference
options.explanation: Heat is a transfer of energy, always hot-to-cold.

options.text: the same thing as temperature
options.explanation: Temperature measures average particle energy; heat is the energy in transit.

options.text: a fluid stored inside hot objects
options.explanation: The caloric idea is long retired; heat is not a substance.

questions.stem: A gas is heated in a sealed rigid box. What happens to its internal energy?

options.text: it decreases as energy escapes through the walls
options.explanation: Heating adds energy; nothing in the setup drains it faster than it arrives.

options.text: it becomes heat and disappears
options.explanation: Energy is conserved; it is stored, not destroyed.

options.text: it increases — the particles move faster
options.explanation: Heating raises the stored energy; in a rigid box it shows up as kinetic energy.

options.text: it stays the same because the box cannot expand
options.explanation: Fixed volume stops expansion, not the energy gain.

questions.stem: A beaker of water is left standing in a room at constant temperature. Why does the water cool slightly over an hour?

options.text: the slowest molecules escape, lowering the average energy left
options.explanation: It is the fastest molecules that break away from the surface first.

options.text: the water gains energy from the room and heats up
options.explanation: A net gain would raise the temperature, not lower it.

options.text: the beaker shrinks and squeezes the water
options.explanation: No state change of the beaker is involved.

options.text: the fastest molecules escape by evaporation, lowering the average energy left
options.explanation: Selective loss of the most energetic particles drags the mean down.

questions.stem: Which statement links heating to its two possible outcomes?

options.text: heating raises the stored energy, which may warm the system or change its state
options.explanation: Temperature rise and state change are the two channels for the added energy.

options.text: heating always raises the temperature and never changes state
options.explanation: At melting and boiling points the temperature holds still while the state changes.

options.text: heating changes state without touching the stored energy
options.explanation: State changes are powered by the raised internal energy.

options.text: heating only transfers energy between two systems, never within one
options.explanation: A single system can be heated and store the energy internally.

questions.stem: Steam scalds more badly than the same mass of boiling water. Which energy account explains this?

options.text: steam is denser and presses harder on the skin
options.explanation: Steam is less dense than water.

options.text: the steam carries extra energy that it releases while condensing on the skin
options.explanation: Condensation hands back the latent energy absorbed during vaporisation.

options.text: steam particles move faster than boiling-water particles
options.explanation: At 100 °C both have the same average kinetic energy; the difference is the latent store.

options.text: steam has a higher specific heat capacity
options.explanation: The scald comes from latent heat released, not from capacity differences.

questions.stem: State what is meant by the internal energy of a system.
questions.modelAnswer: Internal energy is the total energy stored in the particles of the system — their kinetic energy of motion plus the potential energy of their arrangements and attractions.

questions.stem: State the direction in which heat energy flows between two objects at different temperatures.
questions.modelAnswer: Heat flows from the object at the higher temperature to the object at the lower temperature until their temperatures equalise.

questions.stem: Explain why a cream-haired mammal feels cooler after emerging from a swim even on a warm day.
questions.modelAnswer: Water on the fur evaporates, and evaporation is selective — the most energetic molecules leave the surface first. Removing the fastest particles lowers the average kinetic energy of the molecules that remain, and since temperature tracks that average, the surface cools even while the surrounding air stays warm.

questions.stem: A student weighs a beaker of water, leaves it for a day at constant room temperature, then weighs it again and finds the mass smaller. Explain one correct and one incorrect conclusion the class might draw from the mass loss.
questions.modelAnswer: Correct: the mass difference equals the mass of water that evaporated, because the missing molecules left the surface as vapour. Incorrect: claiming the overall count of water molecules in beaker and air combined decreased — evaporation conserves the molecules, it merely moves them from the beaker into the air.
